chapterNote: Chapter 19 is a loose string of antithetical proverbs circling a handful of themes: the worth of integrity over both wealth and clever speech (vv. 1-2, 22), the fickle friendship that money buys and poverty drives off (vv. 4, 6-7), the ruin and reward that follow a man's words and his self-control (vv. 5, 9, 11, 19, 28-29), the discipline that shapes a son while there is still hope (vv. 18, 20, 25, 27), and the sluggard whose laziness starves him (vv. 15, 24). Threaded through it all is the LORD's quiet sovereignty: He receives the kindness shown to the poor as a loan made to Himself (v. 17), He stands behind the prudent wife (v. 14), His counsel alone outlasts a man's many plans (v. 21), and the fear of Him leads to a settled, untroubled life (v. 23).

1.text: Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than one whose lips are twisted and who is a fool.
1.amp: Better [tov — good, the more excellent thing] is a poor man [rush — one who is destitute] who walks [halak — whose whole manner of life moves] in his integrity [tom — wholeness, a life with no hidden seam] than one who is perverse [crooked] in his lips and is a fool [kesil — the thick-headed who scorns correction].
1.notes: tom (H8537) is integrity, the same wholeness commended in 2:7 — a life without a hidden crack. The proverb weighs honest poverty against deceitful folly and finds the poor man heavier: character, not bank account, sets a man's true worth (cf. Prov 28:6). kesil (H3684) is the dull fool who hates being corrected.

2.text: Zeal without knowledge is not good, and the man who rushes ahead with his feet misses the way and sins.
2.amp: It is not good [tov] for the soul [nephesh — the whole eager self] to be without knowledge [daat — discernment]; and he who hurries [uts — presses and urges himself onward] with his feet [regel] misses the way and sins [chet — falls short, steps wrong].
2.notes: nephesh (H5315) here is the appetite, the driving self; daat (H1847) is discernment. To pour out energy without knowledge is dangerous: uts (H213), to press and hasten, paired with the foot, pictures the man who runs before he has looked. Eagerness untethered from wisdom does not merely fail — it sins (chet, H2398), wandering off the mark.

3.text: A man's own folly ruins his way, and then his heart rages against the LORD.
3.amp: The foolishness [ivvelet — moral folly] of man [adam] perverts [overturns, subverts] his way [derek — the road of his life], and his heart [leb] rages [against the LORD, fuming and indignant] against the LORD [YHWH].
3.notes: ivvelet (H200) is folly with a moral edge, not mere ignorance. The cruel irony the proverb exposes: a man wrecks his own derek (H1870) by his folly, then turns and fumes at God for the wreckage. Sin first ruins us, then teaches us to blame heaven; cf. Gen 3:12, where Adam (adam, H120) faults God for the woman.

4.text: Wealth gathers many friends, but the poor man is deserted even by the one friend he had.
4.amp: Wealth [hon — riches, substance] adds [yasaph — keeps increasing] many [rav] friends [rea — companions], but the poor man [dal — the low and weak] is separated [parad — split off, divided away] from his neighbor [rea — the very friend he had].
4.notes: hon (H1952) is substance; the same word for friend (rea, H7453) stands at both ends of the verse, sharpening the contrast. Money draws a crowd of companions (yasaph, H3254, keeps adding them), but poverty (dal, H1800) drives off (parad, H6504) even the last one. The world's friendship follows the wallet, not the man.

5.text: No acquittal awaits the witness who testifies falsely, and the man who keeps puffing out lies finds no way of slipping free.
5.amp: A false [sheqer — deceptive, a deliberate falsehood] witness [ed] will not be held innocent [naqah — cleared, let off as guiltless], and he who pours out [breathes, puffs out] lies [kazab] will not escape [malat — slip away, be delivered].
5.notes: naqah (H5352) is to be acquitted; the KJV margin reads 'held innocent.' This is courtroom language — the ninth commandment with teeth. The verse pairs with v.9, where the same false witness does not merely fail to escape but perishes (abad). malat (H4422) is to slip out of a trap; the liar will find no such slip.

6.text: Many court the favor of a generous ruler, and everyone is a friend to the man who hands out gifts.
6.amp: Many [rav] will entreat [chalah — seek favor, soften the face of] the favor [panim — the face, the gracious presence] of the prince [nadiv — the noble, the generous-hearted]; and every man is a friend [rea] to the man who gives gifts [mattan — something handed over freely].
6.notes: to entreat the panim (H6440), the 'face,' is to seek someone's gracious presence; chalah (H2470) literally softens or sweetens that face. nadiv (H5081) carries both senses 'noble' and 'generous.' The proverb names a hard truth about human nature, echoing v.4: gifts (mattan, H4976) buy a crowd of friends, but such friendship is bought, not given.

7.text: All the brothers of a poor man hate him — how much more do his friends keep their distance! He pursues them with pleading words, but they are nowhere to be found.
7.amp: All the brethren [ach — kinsmen] of the poor [rush] hate [sane — turn against in hostility] him; how much more do his friends [companions] go far [rachaq — keep their distance, remove themselves] from him! He pursues [radaph — chases after] them with words [emer — pleas], yet they are gone.
7.notes: the proverb climbs by lesser-to-greater logic: if even kinsmen (ach, H251) recoil (sane, H8130) from poverty, friends withdraw all the more (rachaq, H7368). The poor man chases (radaph, H7291) after them with words of appeal (emer, H561), but the friendships money bought (vv.4, 6) have evaporated. The Hebrew of the last line is broken and difficult — the very syntax seems to trail off as the friends do.

8.text: He who gets wisdom loves his own soul; he who guards understanding will find what is good.
8.amp: He who gets [qanah — acquires, takes possession of] wisdom [the KJV margin reads 'an heart,' leb — sense, good judgment] loves [ahab — delights in, seeks the good of] his own soul [nephesh]; he who keeps [shamar — guards and preserves] understanding [tebunah — discernment] shall find [matsa] good [tov].
8.notes: the Hebrew literally says he 'gets a heart' (leb, H3820) — in Proverbs the heart is the seat of practical sense, so to get a heart is to gain wisdom. qanah (H7069) is to acquire by effort. The proverb reframes self-love rightly: the truest kindness a man can do himself (ahab, H157, his own nephesh) is to seek wisdom; cf. 8:35-36.

9.text: No acquittal awaits the witness who testifies falsely, and the man who keeps puffing out lies goes down to ruin.
9.amp: A false [sheqer] witness [ed] will not be held innocent [naqah], and he who pours out lies [kazab] shall perish [abad — be destroyed, come to ruin].
9.notes: a near-twin of v.5, but the ending darkens: where v.5 said the liar finds no way of slipping free (malat), here he shall perish (abad, H6). The repetition with intensification is deliberate — the deceiver does not merely fail to flee judgment; he is undone by it. God's court will not be mocked (cf. Deut 19:18-19).

10.text: Soft living sits wrong on a fool — and it is stranger still when a servant holds command over nobles.
10.amp: Delicate living [luxury, soft indulgence] is not seemly [naveh — fitting, comely, in keeping] for a fool [kesil]; stranger still for a servant [ebed — a slave] to hold command [mashal — exercise dominion, govern] over nobles [sar — officials, princes].
10.notes: naveh (H5000) is what is fitting or comely — the proverb judges by a sense of moral fittingness. Luxury wasted on a fool and authority handed to a slave over his betters are both things out of order, the world turned upside-down (cf. Prov 30:21-22; Eccl 10:7). mashal (H4910) is to rule; sar (H8269) are the rightful nobles.

11.text: A man's good sense makes him slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense.
11.amp: The discretion [sekhel — prudence, good sense] of a man [adam] makes him long [arak — to draw out, prolong] in his anger [aph — the flaring nostril, hot wrath]; and it is his glory [tipharet — beauty, splendor] to pass over [abar — cross by, let go past] a transgression [pesha — rebellion, offense].
11.notes: to be 'long' (arak, H748) in anger is to be slow to it — the patient man stretches out the fuse. aph (H639) is literally the nostril, the seat of flaring wrath. Strikingly, restraint is called the man's tipharet (H8597), his glory and beauty: it is no weakness but splendor to let an offense (pesha, H6588) pass by; cf. Prov 16:32; Matt 5:39.

12.text: The king's rage is like the roar of a lion, but his favor is like dew upon the grass.
12.amp: The king's wrath is as the roaring of a lion; but his favor [ratzon — delight, good pleasure, acceptance] is as dew [tal — the night dew] upon the grass [eseb — green herbage].
12.notes: two images of a king's power, terrible and tender. The lion's roar signals deadly danger; tal (H2919), the dew, signals quiet, life-giving refreshment in a dry land. ratzon (H7522), favor, is the king's good pleasure that revives like dew on parched grass (eseb, H6212). The proverb teaches reverent wisdom toward authority — and hints at the King of kings, whose favor is life (Ps 30:5).

13.text: A foolish son is his father's ruin, and a wife's quarreling is a roof that never stops dripping.
13.amp: A foolish [kesil] son [ben] is the calamity [havvah — engulfing ruin, destruction] of his father [ab]; and the contentions [quarrels, strife] of a wife [ishshah] are a continual [tarad — driving on without pause] dripping [a leaking roof].
13.notes: two domestic miseries set side by side: the kesil (H3684) son who is his father's (ab, H1) havvah (H1942), engulfing disaster, and the quarrelsome wife whose strife is like a roof leak that never lets up (tarad, H2956, drives on relentlessly). The home, meant to be a refuge, becomes a slow torment; cf. Prov 27:15. Both proverbs press the worth of wisdom in those nearest us.

14.text: From his fathers a man may inherit a house and riches, but a wife of sound judgment is the LORD's own gift.
14.amp: House [bayith] and riches [hon — wealth, substance] come down as the inheritance [nachalah — the heritage passed down] of fathers [ab]; but a wife [ishshah] of sound judgment [sakal — prudent, wise, insightful, one who acts with skill] is from the LORD [YHWH] Himself.
14.notes: the verse draws a deliberate line: lands and goods come down the family tree as nachalah (H5159), inherited heritage, but a wise wife (sakal, H7919, one of good sense) is a direct gift from the LORD's own hand. Set against v.13's quarrelsome wife, this is the better portion — and no human inheritance can secure it. Marriage rightly received is providence, not luck (cf. Prov 18:22).

15.text: Laziness drops a man into deep sleep, and the slack soul goes hungry.
15.amp: Slothfulness [laziness, sluggishness] casts [naphal — makes to fall, throws down] into a deep sleep [tardemah — a heavy, trance-like slumber]; and an idle [remiyah — slack, negligent, deceitful in effort] soul [nephesh] shall suffer hunger.
15.notes: tardemah (H8639) is the deep stupor that fell on Adam and on Abram (Gen 2:21; 15:12) — here it is the sluggard's self-induced coma. remiyah (H7423) means slackness with a hint of deceit, work done with a loose hand. The proverb traces a plain line of cause and effect: laziness fells a man into sleep, and the slack soul (nephesh, H5315) wakes to an empty stomach; cf. Prov 6:9-11.

16.text: He who keeps the commandment keeps his own soul; he who is careless of his ways will die.
16.amp: He who keeps [shamar — guards, observes] the commandment [mitsvah — the charge, the command] keeps [shamar] his own soul [nephesh]; but he who despises [bazah — holds in contempt, treats as worthless] his ways [derek] shall die.
16.notes: the verse turns on the doubled shamar (H8104): keep the mitsvah (H4687) and you keep yourself. To despise (bazah, H959) one's own ways is to live carelessly, treating one's conduct as not worth watching — and such carelessness is fatal. Obedience is not a cage but a guard upon the soul (nephesh, H5315); cf. Luke 11:28.

17.text: He who shows favor to the poor lends to the LORD, and the LORD will repay him for his kindness.
17.amp: He who has pity [chanan — shows grace and favor] upon the poor [dal — the low and weak] lends [lavah — joins himself by a loan] unto the LORD [YHWH]; and that which he has given [gemul — his good deed, the benefit done] He will repay him [shalam — make full, render in full, pay back].
17.notes: one of Scripture's most astonishing claims about charity: kindness (chanan, H2603) to the poor (dal, H1800) is reckoned by God as a personal loan to Himself (lavah, H3867). And the LORD pays His debts in full — shalam (H7999), to make whole, render complete. The poor man's empty hands are God's collection plate, and heaven keeps the books; cf. Matt 25:40; 2 Cor 9:6-8.

18.text: Discipline your son while there is still hope, and do not set your heart on his destruction.
18.amp: Chasten [yasar — discipline, correct, instruct] your son [ben] while there is [yesh — while it still exists] hope [tikvah — expectation, a cord to hold to], and do not lift up your soul [nephesh — the KJV margin: do not spare to his destruction] to his crying.
18.notes: tikvah (H8615) is hope, from a root meaning a cord or line — there is still a tie to take hold of while the child is young. yasar (H3256) is formative discipline, the loving correction of 1:8. The difficult second line warns the parent not to let indulgent pity become a party to the child's ruin — to withhold correction is, in the end, to consent to his death; cf. Prov 13:24; 23:13-14.

19.text: A man of great wrath must pay the penalty; rescue him once, and you will only have to do it again.
19.amp: A man of great [gadol — large, mighty in measure] wrath [chemah — hot fury, the boiling-over of temper] shall bear [nasa — lift up and carry] the penalty; for if you deliver [natsal — snatch him out] him, yet you must do it again [yasaph — add to it, repeat].
19.notes: chemah (H2534) is wrath as heat, the temper that boils over; such a man must carry (nasa, H5375) the consequences his rage brings on. The proverb's wisdom is hard but kind: rescue (natsal, H5337) a hot-tempered man from one self-made disaster and you sign up to do it again (yasaph, H3254) — repeated bailouts only shield him from the discipline he needs. Some men must feel the weight of their own anger to be cured of it.

20.text: Listen to counsel and accept correction, that you may grow wise in the end.
20.amp: Hear [shama — listen and heed] counsel [etsah — advice, wise guidance], and receive [accept, take in] instruction [musar — corrective discipline], that you may be wise [chakam — become wise, act with wisdom] in your latter end [acharit — the after-time, the final outcome of life].
20.notes: shama (H8085) is hearing that obeys, not bare listening; musar (H4148) is the corrective instruction that runs through the whole book (1:2). The reward is set in the acharit (H319), the latter end — wisdom is a long game, and the youth who takes correction now is laying up sense for the man he will become. Wisdom received early bears its fruit at the finish; cf. Prov 1:5; 12:15.

21.text: Many are the plans in a man's heart, but it is the counsel of the LORD that will stand.
21.amp: There are many [rav] devices [machashabah — thoughts, schemes, plans] in a man's [ish] heart [leb]; nevertheless the counsel [etsah — the settled purpose] of the LORD [YHWH], that shall stand [qum — rise up and remain firm].
21.notes: machashabah (H4284) is the busy plotting of the human heart (leb, H3820); etsah (H6098), counsel, is the same word used of the wise advice we are told to hear in v.20 — but here it is the LORD's counsel, set over against all our scheming. Man proposes in many plans; God disposes in one, and His alone stands firm (qum, H6965); cf. Prov 16:9; Isa 46:10; Acts 5:38-39.

22.text: What is desired in a man is his kindness, and a poor man is better than a liar.
22.amp: The desire [taavah — what is longed for, found desirable] of a man [adam] is his kindness [chesed — steadfast love, loyal goodness]; and a poor man [rush] is better [tov] than a liar [kazab — a man of falsehood].
22.notes: chesed (H2617) is covenant loyalty and steadfast love — the proverb says what makes a man truly desirable (taavah, H8378) is not his wealth but his loyal kindness. The second line returns to the theme of v.1: honest poverty (rush, H7326) outranks prosperous deceit (kazab, H3577). Better to be poor with chesed than rich with a lie.

23.text: The fear of the LORD leads to life; he who has it rests content and will not be visited by harm.
23.amp: The fear [yirah — reverent awe] of the LORD [YHWH] tends to life [chay — toward life, living]; and he who has it shall abide [lun — lodge, spend the night, rest] satisfied; he shall not be visited [paqad — mustered for, appointed to] with evil [ra — harm, calamity].
23.notes: yirat YHWH (H3374 + H3068), the fear of the LORD, is the book's master theme (1:7), and here its fruit is chay (H2416), life itself. The man who has it lodges (lun, H3885) for the night satisfied and secure — a settled, restful contentment. paqad (H6485) is to visit or appoint; no evil (ra, H7451) is mustered against him. The fear of God is the gateway to a life unafraid; cf. Ps 25:12-13; Prov 14:27.

24.text: Once the sluggard has sunk his hand down into the bowl, he cannot rouse himself to lift it back up to his own mouth.
24.amp: A slothful [atsel — the sluggard, the lazy man] man hides [taman — buries, conceals] his hand in his bosom [the dish, the bowl], and will not so much as bring [shub — return, bring back] it to his mouth [peh] again [shub].
24.notes: the proverb is comic hyperbole to make laziness ridiculous: the atsel (H6102), sluggard, has plunged (taman, H2934, buried) his hand in the food but is too slack even to lift it back (shub, H7725) to his mouth (peh, H6310). Laziness is so total it will not finish the simplest act for its own benefit; cf. Prov 26:15. The sluggard starves with the meal in front of him.

25.text: Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence; rebuke a man of understanding, and he will gain knowledge.
25.amp: Smite [nakah — strike, flog] a scorner [luts — the mocker who scoffs at correction], and the simple [peti — the naive, easily-led] will beware [the KJV margin: will become shrewd, take warning]; and reprove [yakach — correct, rebuke with argument] one who has understanding [biyn — one who discerns], and he will understand [biyn] knowledge [daat].
25.notes: three kinds of men respond to three levels of correction. The luts (H3887), scoffer, is past instruction — you punish him not to mend him but so the watching peti (H6612), the naive, learns by his example. But the man of discernment (biyn, H995) needs only a word (yakach, H3198) and grows by it. The wise are improved by a rebuke that the fool only resents; cf. Prov 9:8-9; 17:10.

26.text: He who assaults his father and drives away his mother is a son who brings shame and disgrace.
26.amp: He who wastes [assaults, violently robs] his father [ab], and chases away [barach — makes to flee, drives off] his mother [em], is a son [ben] who causes shame [bosh — brings to disgrace] and brings reproach [khapher — causes to blush, makes confounded].
26.notes: to drive a mother out (barach, H1272, to make flee) and rob a father is a grotesque inversion of the fifth commandment. Such a son is doubly named: he causes shame (bosh, H954) and brings reproach (khapher, H2659) — two near-synonyms for public disgrace, heaped up to show how far below contempt he has fallen. The proverb measures a man by how he treats those who gave him life; cf. Prov 20:20; 30:17.

27.text: Stop listening, my son, to instruction, and you will only stray from the words of knowledge.
27.amp: Cease [chadal — stop, leave off, desist], my son [ben], to hear [shama] the instruction [musar — corrective teaching] that causes you to stray from the words [emer — sayings] of knowledge [daat].
27.notes: the verse is pointed irony, a warning by way of its opposite: if you quit listening (chadal, H2308, leave off) to musar (H4148), the only direction left is away — you will wander from the emer (H561), the words of knowledge (daat, H1847). To stop learning is not to stand still but to drift backward. The teacher's affectionate 'my son' (ben, H1121) makes the caution tender, not harsh; cf. Prov 4:1-2.

28.text: A worthless witness scoffs at justice, and the mouth of the wicked gulps down iniquity.
28.amp: An ungodly [beliyyaal — worthless, of Belial, utterly base] witness [ed] scorns [luts — mocks, makes a jest of] judgment [mishpat — justice, the right verdict]; and the mouth [peh] of the wicked [rasha — the guilty, the lawless] devours [bala — swallows, gulps down] iniquity [aven — wickedness, trouble].
28.notes: beliyyaal (H1100), 'of Belial,' is the strongest word for moral worthlessness (the KJV margin reads 'a witness of Belial'). Such a witness mocks (luts, H3887) the very justice (mishpat, H4941) he is sworn to serve. The wicked man's mouth (peh, H6310) does not merely speak evil but swallows it (bala, H1104) like food — iniquity (aven, H205) is his appetite, his daily bread; cf. Job 15:16; Prov 4:17.

29.text: Judgments stand ready for scoffers, and a beating for the backs of fools.
29.amp: Judgments [shephet — acts of judgment, sentences] are prepared [kun — established, made ready and firm] for scorners [luts — the mockers], and stripes [the rod's blows] for the back [gev] of fools [kesil].
29.notes: the chapter closes on the certainty of reckoning: shephet (H8201), executed judgments, are fixed and ready (kun, H3559, firmly established) for the scoffer (luts, H3887), and the rod waits for the fool's back (gev, H1460). The mocker who laughs at correction (v.28) and the kesil (H3684) who refuses it will meet the discipline they spurned — now as punishment rather than instruction; cf. Prov 10:13; 26:3.
